Analysis, Measurement & Execution

Captain Track NFPA 1021 FO II–III

Chapter 13B · Lesson 1 of 5

Reading Your Environment
SWOT & PESTLE Analysis

⏱ 20 min · 🔍 Environmental Analysis · Strategic Diagnosis
Fast Track
Frameworks + OB cards only

Before you plan, you assess. SWOT and PESTLE are the two environmental scanning tools used at the organizational level — SWOT for internal and external factors you can directly observe, PESTLE for the macro-environment forces shaping the context your organization operates in. Used together, they produce a complete picture of strategic position.

S — Strengths
Internal, positive. Genuine capabilities that provide competitive advantage. Build on these.
Fire/EMS: Clinical outcomes, specialized team capability, community trust, response times
W — Weaknesses
Internal, negative. Capability gaps or liabilities. Honest self-assessment required.
Fire/EMS: Succession gaps, aging fleet, training deficits, documentation compliance
O — Opportunities
External, positive. Environmental factors the organization can leverage. Time-limited.
Fire/EMS: Grant windows, annexation, political alignment, community health funding
T — Threats
External, negative. Environmental factors that require mitigation or monitoring.
Fire/EMS: Budget cuts, population growth outpacing resources, recruitment competition, call volume shift

PESTLE — The External Environment in Six Dimensions

SWOT Opportunities and Threats are specific to your organization. PESTLE is the broader context — the forces your organization doesn't control but must account for in any strategic plan. A department that builds a 5-year workforce plan without analyzing the Economic and Social dimensions of their region is planning in a vacuum.

P
Political
Government policy, labor law, election cycles, budget authority.
City council priorities, CBA environment, annexation policy
E
Economic
Budget cycles, property tax base, cost of labor and apparatus.
Recession cuts, overtime pressure, apparatus lifecycle costs
S
Social
Demographics, community expectations, workforce generational shifts.
Aging population, mental health call volume, recruitment diversity
T
Technological
Emerging technology, data analytics, telemedicine capability.
ePCR systems, predictive deployment, CAD integration
L
Legal
NFPA compliance, liability, medical director scope, labor law.
NFPA 1710/1720 staffing, HIPAA, scope of practice authority
E
Environmental
Climate, geography, natural disaster risk, wildland interface.
WUI growth, extreme heat EMS surges, drought conditions

Using Both Together

PESTLE feeds SWOT. Your PESTLE analysis of Technological change (ePCR, predictive deployment) directly informs your SWOT Opportunities column. Your PESTLE analysis of Political trends (city council priorities, upcoming election) informs your SWOT Threats column. Run PESTLE first to populate the external half of your SWOT.

Oral Board — Environmental Analysis
BC Level
"You've been given the BC position. Before you propose any strategic changes, how do you assess where the organization stands?"
This is a SWOT + PESTLE question. Name both frameworks, describe what data you'd gather for each dimension, and explain how you'd use the analysis before making recommendations.
Lesson 1 — Key Takeaways
SWOT: internal (Strengths/Weaknesses) + external (Opportunities/Threats). Start with honest internal assessment.
PESTLE: six macro-environment dimensions — Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental.
Sequence: run PESTLE first to populate the external side of SWOT. PESTLE is the context; SWOT is the diagnosis.

Chapter 13B · Lesson 2 of 5

Measuring & Aligning
Balanced Scorecard + McKinsey 7-S

⏱ 22 min · 📊 Measurement + Alignment · Two Power Tools
Fast Track
Frameworks + OB cards only

Fire departments measure response times with extraordinary precision and almost nothing else. The Balanced Scorecard fixes that by requiring measurement across four organizational dimensions simultaneously. The McKinsey 7-S framework explains why strategies fail even when the goals are right — seven elements must be aligned, not just one.

The Balanced Scorecard — Four Perspectives

Kaplan and Norton developed the BSC at Harvard in 1992 to solve one specific problem: organizations that optimized for one metric while the metrics that determined long-term performance went unmeasured. In fire service, that unmeasured metric is consistently Learning and Growth — the perspective most neglected and most predictive.

💰
Perspective 1 — Financial / Stewardship
Are we responsible stewards of public resources?
Budget variance, cost-per-unit-hour, overtime rate, apparatus lifecycle costs, grant utilization. The fire service equivalent of financial performance is organizational sustainability.
🏘️
Perspective 2 — Community / Customer
Are we serving the community effectively and equitably?
Response time performance, ROSC rates, cardiac arrest survival, community satisfaction, CRR program outcomes, service equity across districts. Where Greenleaf's question is answered with data.
⚙️
Perspective 3 — Internal Processes
Are our systems and processes delivering?
Training completion, documentation accuracy, near-miss reporting rate, protocol compliance, QI review turnaround. Process quality is a leading indicator of outcome quality.
🌱
Perspective 4 — Learning & Growth
Are we building capacity for the future?
Succession readiness, promotion rate, voluntary turnover, advanced certification rate, innovation adoption. The most neglected perspective — and the most predictive of long-term organizational health.

McKinsey 7-S — Why Good Strategies Fail

Peters and Waterman developed 7-S at McKinsey in 1980 to answer a question strategic planning consistently left unanswered: why do good strategies fail in execution? Their finding: because strategy is only one of seven elements that must be aligned. When any element is misaligned, organizational energy is spent managing the conflict rather than advancing the strategy.

The Fulcrum — Drives All Other Elements
Shared Values
Hard Element
Strategy
The plan — direction and resource allocation. Most visible, most commonly over-weighted in fire service.
Hard Element
Structure
Command hierarchy, span of control, district assignments, functional divisions.
Hard Element
Systems
Daily processes — CAD, EMS protocols, training systems, scheduling, documentation.
Soft Element
Style
Leadership culture — how command actually behaves, not the org chart.
Soft Element
Staff
The people — capabilities, experience, development needs, retention.
Soft Element
Skills
Organizational competencies — clinical excellence, community trust, tactical capability.
Board diagnostic: A Chief who changes Strategy, Structure, and Systems but leaves Shared Values and Style unchanged will watch the new strategy get absorbed by culture until it resembles the old one.
Oral Board — Measurement + Alignment
BC Level
"Your organization has excellent response times but high turnover, low morale, and declining community trust. How do you diagnose this situation?"
BSC + 7-S combined. The response time metric is one BSC dimension (Community/Process). The turnover and morale are Learning & Growth (BSC) and Staff/Shared Values (7-S). Name both frameworks and show how they connect.
Lesson 2 — Key Takeaways
BSC: four perspectives — Financial/Stewardship, Community, Internal Processes, Learning & Growth. Measure all four or you're flying blind.
7-S: three Hard elements (Strategy, Structure, Systems) + four Soft elements (Style, Staff, Skills, Shared Values). Culture absorbs strategy when Soft elements aren't aligned.
Board power move: use BSC to identify WHAT is underperforming, then use 7-S to diagnose WHY.

Chapter 13B · Lesson 3 of 5

CRR, OODA & AAR
Prevention, Decision Speed & Learning

⏱ 24 min · 🏘 NFPA 1300 · Boyd · Just Culture
Fast Track
Frameworks + OB cards only

Three frameworks that address different strategic challenges: the Five E's of Community Risk Reduction addresses what your organization is doing to prevent the emergencies it responds to; the OODA Loop addresses how fast your organization can process information and adapt; and the After Action Review is the mechanism that converts experience into organizational learning.

Community Risk Reduction — The Five E's (NFPA 1300)

NFPA 1300 codifies Community Risk Reduction as the strategic approach to reducing injury and death through intervention before the emergency occurs. The Five E's are the intervention strategies — and they are explicitly ranked by leverage. Emergency Response is the last resort, not the primary strategy.

E
Education
Knowledge and awareness campaigns. Smoke detector programs, car seat safety, fall prevention.
Most scalable — highest reach per dollar.
E
Engineering
Built-environment changes that reduce hazard without requiring behavior change.
Highest sustained impact — works after installation.
E
Enforcement
Code compliance, inspections, permit processes, occupancy standards.
Most authority-dependent — requires political will.
E
Economics
Financial incentives and disincentives that change behavior at scale.
Especially effective in commercial occupancies.
E
Emergency Response
Traditional fire/EMS role — response after the event occurs.
Lowest leverage. The other four E's exist to reduce this one.

OODA — Organizational Decision Speed

Colonel John Boyd developed the OODA Loop from analysis of fighter pilot engagement — the pilot who could cycle through the loop faster consistently won regardless of the quality of their aircraft. At the organizational level, the OODA Loop describes how quickly your organization can observe a change in environment, orient to its significance, decide on a response, and act. The bottleneck is almost always Orient.

O
Observe
Unfiltered data from the environment. Quality determined by the organizational culture of honest reporting — not filtered for leadership comfort.
O
Orient
The bottleneck. Shaped by mental models, experience, culture, and analysis. Where most organizations slow down or distort reality.
D
Decide
Select from options orientation generates. A good decision now beats a perfect decision late. Commit and revisit in the next loop.
A
Act
Execute and generate new observations. The loop restarts. Faster loop wins — not faster acting, faster cycling through all four stages.
Strategic application: The organization with the faster OODA loop gets inside the adversary's decision cycle — whether that's a fire environment, a public health threat, or a budget negotiation.

The AAR as Strategic Learning Infrastructure

The After Action Review is the mechanism by which organizations learn from experience rather than just accumulating it. Used consistently, it builds the Learning and Growth BSC perspective. The three questions are deceptively simple — the difficulty is creating the psychological safety for honest answers to Question 2.

After Action Review — Three Questions
Question 1
What did we intend to happen?
The plan, objective, and success criterion. Name it before discussing outcomes — otherwise the AAR becomes revisionist.
Question 2
What actually happened?
Facts only — no blame, no defense. The AAR fails when this becomes a defense hearing instead of a fact-finding conversation.
Question 3
What will we do differently?
Specific changes to process, training, or systems. Not "try harder" — named changes that address the identified gap.
Board: The AAR demonstrates Just Culture + systems thinking + continuous improvement — score target 5/5 at BC level
Oral Board — CRR + Learning Systems
Captain Level
"Response volume in your district has increased 40% over five years with the same staffing. What is your strategic response?"
This is a CRR + OODA question. The tactical answer is more staffing. The strategic answer starts with CRR — which of the Five E's can reduce the demand? Then OODA — how does your organization learn fast enough to adapt?
Lesson 3 — Key Takeaways
Five E's (NFPA 1300): Education, Engineering, Enforcement, Economics, Emergency Response. Emergency Response has the lowest leverage — the other four exist to reduce the need for it.
OODA: Observe → Orient → Decide → Act. The bottleneck is Orient. Faster loop wins — not faster acting.
AAR: three questions — What did we plan? What happened? What changes? The third question is the whole point.

The 90-Day Entry Plan
Your Strategic First 90 Days

⏱ 22 min · 📅 The Most Common Board Question · Entry Strategy
Fast Track
Frameworks + OB cards only

The 90-Day Entry Plan question appears in nearly every BC and Chief-level assessment center. It is not asking what you will change — it is asking whether you have the strategic discipline to listen before you act. The candidate who says "I'd make immediate changes to X" scores poorly. The candidate who describes a structured assessment, listening, and alignment process scores well.

The Three-Phase Framework

The 90-day structure is not about speed — it is about sequence. Organizations have changed new leaders' priorities before they even know what the real priorities are. The three-phase framework protects against premature action while creating a visible, credible process that builds trust with the organization.

Days 1–30 · Listen & Assess
No major changes. No direction announcements.
SWOT + PESTLE assessment
One-on-ones with every supervisor
BSC baseline — what are we actually measuring?
Identify the cultural current (what does the org believe about itself?)
Output: A written organizational assessment. No recommendations yet.
Days 31–60 · Analyze & Connect
Share findings. Test assumptions. Build alignment.
Present SWOT findings to leadership team
Identify the 2–3 highest-leverage strategic gaps
Connect gaps to the existing Mission and Vision
Run 7-S misalignment diagnostic
Output: A prioritized gap analysis with stakeholder input.
Days 61–90 · Draft & Align
First strategic priorities. Collaborative development.
Draft top 3 strategic goals with measurable objectives
Define the BSC metrics for each goal
Build 90-day action plan with owners and deadlines
Communicate direction to full organization
Output: A one-page strategic direction document. First public commitment.

Why This Structure Scores Well

Assessment center assessors are looking for four things in a 90-day response: organizational humility (you don't arrive knowing all the answers), systematic approach (structured process, not ad hoc), stakeholder inclusion (you build alignment before announcing direction), and specificity (concrete deliverables, not vague intentions). The three-phase framework delivers all four.

The 90-Day Critical Rule

No major changes in the first 30 days. This is the most important constraint in the framework. A new BC who reorganizes the shift structure on Day 5 has made a decision before gathering data. Even if the decision is right, the process signals poor strategic judgment — and in assessment centers, process is what's being scored.

Oral Board — 90-Day Entry Plan
BC / Chief Level
"You've been selected. Walk me through your first 90 days."
Use the three-phase framework. Name the phases, describe the deliverable for each, and emphasize that you will not announce strategic direction until Day 61+ after completing the assessment and alignment phases.
Lesson 4 — Key Takeaways
Days 1–30: Listen and assess. SWOT + PESTLE + one-on-ones. No major changes. Written organizational assessment as output.
Days 31–60: Analyze and connect. Share findings, identify gaps, run 7-S diagnostic. Stakeholder input before direction-setting.
Days 61–90: Draft and align. Top 3 strategic goals, BSC metrics, 90-day action plan with owners. First public strategic commitment.

Chapter 13B Capstone
All Six Frameworks in One Scenario

⏱ 20 min · 🎯 Integration · Full Framework Map · Board-Ready
Fast Track
Frameworks + OB cards only

Strategic planning tools are only valuable when you can deploy them under pressure in combination — not as isolated definitions. This capstone lesson shows how all six Chapter 13B frameworks work together in a single board scenario, and how to sequence them for maximum impact.

The Framework Map — How the Tools Connect

Phase 1 — Diagnose
SWOT + PESTLE
Where are we? What are our strengths, gaps, opportunities, and threats? What macro forces are shaping our environment?
Phase 2 — Measure
Balanced Scorecard
What are we actually tracking? Which of the four perspectives is most underdeveloped? Where is the measurement gap?
Phase 3 — Align
McKinsey 7-S
Are our seven elements aligned to execute the strategy? Where is the friction? Is it a Hard element or a Soft element failure?
Phase 4 — Reduce Risk
CRR + Five E's
Are we addressing root causes or just responding to outcomes? Which E's are we deploying? Which have the highest leverage?
Phase 5 — Adapt Fast
OODA Loop
How quickly can the organization observe changes, orient to them, and act? Is orientation being distorted by culture or hierarchy?
Phase 6 — Learn
AAR + 90-Day Plan
Are we converting experience into improvement? Is the entry process creating the data foundation needed for strategic decisions?

The Full Scenario — Applied Together

Sample BC-Level Board Scenario

"You've been selected as the new BC for a struggling division. Response times are good, but morale is low, turnover is high, and the community has filed two formal complaints about the medical response quality. You have 90 days before your first formal review with the Chief. Walk me through your approach."

SWOT: Good response times (Strength). Turnover and morale (Weakness). Community complaints (external signal — SWOT Threat, PESTLE Social dimension).
BSC: Community and Learning & Growth perspectives are underdeveloped — the two worst things to neglect simultaneously.
7-S: Morale = Shared Values + Style misalignment. High turnover = Staff and Skills gap. These are Soft element failures — a structural fix won't solve them.
CRR: Medical response quality complaints may indicate a process gap addressable through internal Engineering (systems/protocols) or Education (crew-level training).
90-Day: Phase 1 focuses entirely on listening before recommending changes. The diagnosis above is the starting hypothesis, not the conclusion.

Oral Board — Full Integration
Chief Level
"What is your strategic planning process? Walk me from assessment to execution."
This is asking you to narrate the entire framework map. SWOT + PESTLE → BSC → 7-S → CRR/Five E's → OODA → AAR → 90-Day entry. You don't need to use all six in every scenario — but you need to know which to deploy and when.
Chapter 13B — Complete
SWOT + PESTLE: diagnose strategic position. Run PESTLE first to populate the external side of SWOT.
BSC: measure all four perspectives. Learning & Growth is most neglected and most predictive.
7-S: Hard elements are visible and changeable; Soft elements are invisible and powerful. Culture absorbs strategy.
Five E's: Prevention hierarchy — Emergency Response has the lowest leverage of the five.
OODA + AAR: decision speed + organizational learning. The Orient bottleneck. The third AAR question is the whole point.
90-Day: listen before acting. No major changes in Days 1–30. Output-driven phases.

Knowledge Check
Five questions across the chapter. Pick an answer to see the reasoning. No score, no penalty — this is retrieval practice: testing is learning.
1. You need to understand the outside forces shaping your district before setting strategy. Which tool is the dedicated six-force scan of the external environment?
2. In a SWOT analysis, Strengths and Weaknesses are ___, while Opportunities and Threats are ___.
3. A department posts excellent response-time numbers, but morale and community trust are eroding. Which tool is built to stop leaders from over-optimizing one metric by balancing multiple perspectives?
4. In the OODA loop, which phase is the decisive one — where the experienced officer’s pattern library filters raw observations through mental models?
